content: Vegetarian cuisine is defined as food that adheres to vegetarian principles by excluding meat and animal-derived tissue products. For lacto-ovo vegetarians, the most common type of vegetarianism in Western cultures, the consumption of dairy products such as milk, cheese, and eggs is allowed. Veganism, the strictest form of vegetarianism, excludes all animal-derived products, including dairy, honey, and even certain refined sugars processed with bone char. Vegetarian foods can be categorized into two main types: traditional vegetarian foods, such as grains, fruits, vegetables, and nuts, and meat analogues, which replicate the taste, texture, and appearance of meat. Vegans may also use substitutes for eggs and dairy products, with tofu and textured vegetable protein (TVP) being common examples of such analogues. Foods Commonly Used in Vegetarian Cuisine Vegetarian cuisine typically includes the following food groups: Cereals and grains: Examples include maize, corn, wheat, rice, barley, sorghum, millet, oats, rye, triticale, buckwheat, fonio, and quinoa, as well as their derivatives like flour, bread, pasta, and baked goods. Vegetables and mushrooms: These can be consumed fresh or pickled. Some strict Indian vegetarians avoid mushrooms. Vegetable-derived products, such as oils and fats, are also included. Fruits: Both fresh and dried fruits are widely consumed. Legumes: This category includes beans (e.g., soybeans and soy-based products like tofu, soy milk, and TVP), chickpeas, peas, lentils, and peanuts. Tree nuts and seeds: These are staples in vegetarian diets. Spices and herbs: Widely used to enhance flavor. Other foods: Examples include olives and seaweed. Dairy products: Milk, butter, cheese, and yogurt are consumed by lacto-ovo vegetarians but are excluded by vegans. Dishes That Are Traditionally Vegetarian Many dishes are inherently vegetarian and do not require ingredient substitutions. These include: Pasta, rice, bean, potato, and bulgur/couscous dishes, as well as stews, soups, and stir-fries. Breakfast items like cereals, oatmeal, granola bars, and donuts. Fresh fruits and most types of salads. Side dishes such as mashed potatoes, scalloped potatoes, seasoned rice, and macaroni and cheese. Snacks and meals like potato salad, baba ganoush, pita wraps, burrito wraps, vegetable pilafs, baked potatoes, fried potato skins with toppings, corn on the cob, and smoothies. Sandwiches, including grilled cheese and cold sandwiches with ingredients like roasted eggplant, mushrooms, bell peppers, cheeses, and avocado. Classical Buddhist cuisine, often served in Asian temples and restaurants near temples, which is entirely vegetarian. Vegetarian Dishes in National Cuisines Vegetarian dishes are prevalent in many national cuisines: Indian cuisine: Vegetarianism is deeply rooted in Indian culture, particularly among Hindu Brahmins. Common vegetarian dishes include pakora, samosa, khichri, pulao, raita, rasam, baingan bharta, chana masala, kormas, sambars, jalfrezis, saag aloo, and various subjis (vegetable dishes) like bhindi subji and gobi subji. South Indian dishes such as dosas, idlis, vadas, sambar, rasam, and chutneys are also popular. Many Indian breads, such as chapati, naan, roti, and parathas, are often stuffed with vegetarian fillings. Spanish cuisine: Vegetarian options include tumbet, polenta, and various tapas dishes. Mexican cuisine: Vegetarian dishes include salsa and guacamole with chips, rice and bean burritos (without lard or chicken fat), quesadillas, bean tacos, chilaquiles, chili without meat, black beans with rice, chiles rellenos, cheese enchiladas, and vegetable fajitas. Italian cuisine: Many pastas, pizzas, eggplant-based dishes like rotini and crostini, bruschetta, and risottos are vegetarian. Continental cuisine: Examples include ratatouille, braised leeks with olives and parsley, quiches, sautéed Swiss chard, vegetable-stuffed mushrooms, and Brussels sprouts with mushrooms and squash. Balkan cuisine: Vegetarian dishes include dolmas and spanakopita. Russian and Slavic cuisine: Soups like vegetable borscht, shchi, and okroshka, as well as pirogi, blini, vareniki, kasha, buckwheat, and fermented or pickled vegetables, are common. Ethiopian cuisine: Many dishes are vegetarian. Middle Eastern cuisine: Popular vegetarian options include falafel, hummus, tahini, minted yogurts, and couscous. Chinese cuisine: Vegetarian dishes often feature mushrooms, noodles, eggplant, string beans, broccoli, rice, tofu, and mixed vegetables. Japanese cuisine: Vegetarian options include tempura, edamame, nameko-jiru, and vegetable sushi. Miso soup, made from fermented soybean paste, is also vegetarian. Thai cuisine: Vegetarian dishes include pad kee mao and various Thai curries. Creole and Southern cuisine: Vegetarian options include hush puppies, okra patties, rice and beans, and sautéed kale or collards (if not cooked with pork fat or meat stock). Welsh cuisine: Examples include Glamorgan sausages, laverbread, and Welsh rarebit. Vegetarian Desserts Many desserts are vegetarian, including pies, cobblers, cakes, brownies, cookies, truffles, rice pudding, ice cream, and crème brûlée. Oriental desserts like halva, lokum (Turkish delight), and baklava are often vegetarian, with some being vegan. Cuisine Using Meat Analogues Vegetarian versions of traditionally meat-based dishes are popular among vegetarians and non-vegetarians alike. These include: Veggie burgers: Made from grains, TVP, seitan, tempeh, or mushrooms. Some burgers are made without mock meat, known as burgerless burgers. Veggie dogs: Typically made from TVP. Imitation sausages: Includes soysage and various types of vegetarian salami, bologna, and pepperoni, often made from soy. Mock meats: Includes meatyballs and vegetarian chicken substitutes made from seitan, tofu, or TVP. Vegetarian jambalaya: Made with mock sausage and chicken, often using TVP, seitan, or tempeh. Tomato omelette: Made with a flour paste and tomatoes, without eggs. Scrambled tofu: Tofu is mashed and fried with spices, often including turmeric for a yellow color, to mimic scrambled eggs. Mycoprotein is another common base for mock meats, with vegetarian flavorings like sea vegetables added to create seafood-like tastes. It is important to note that tofu and tempeh are not always used as meat substitutes but are integral components of certain cuisines.
